summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for a caseworker and a state trooper, holding that removal of all five children was supported by an objectively reasonable suspicion of abuse and an imminent threat of abuse, and that a post-deprivation hearing three business days after the removal satisfied procedural due process.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling First Circuit standard for emergency protective custody: objectively reasonable suspicion of abuse or imminent threat, followed by prompt judicial review.
key_cases.quote: no substantive due process violation is stated if there existed a reasonable suspicion that abuse had occurred or that a threat of abuse was imminent at the time of removal

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a case arising from a New Hampshire DCYS investigation and ex parte removal, the court affirmed dismissal of the 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims against a court-appointed psychologist and her supervisor because the complaint stated no violation of any federal constitutional right, and affirmed dismissal of the state law claims as barred by the reporter immunity of RSA 169-C:31.
key_cases.relevance: Immediate removal was obtained ex parte and executed the same evening, and the court found no federal claim where the State's statutory procedures were followed.
key_cases.quote: the relationship between parent and child may be investigated and terminated by the state provided constitutionally adequate procedures are followed

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that private individuals under contract with the State to perform child abuse counseling and investigation may assert qualified immunity because they are the functional equivalent of public officials, and that they were entitled to it as a matter of law because the right to family integrity was not sufficiently particularized to put them on notice that their conduct was unlawful.
key_cases.relevance: Officials responding to sexual abuse allegations are protected in taking protective steps because the countervailing family integrity right is not clearly defined.
key_cases.quote: the right to family integrity has not been so particularized as to put defendants on notice that their conduct was unlawful

key_cases.case_name: Hatch v. Department for Children, Youth & Their Families (State of Rhode Island)
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that the Constitution permits a caseworker to take a child into temporary custody without a prior hearing when the caseworker has a reasonable suspicion that abuse has occurred or that a threat of abuse is imminent, and affirmed the denial of leave to amend because the caseworker had such a suspicion and was entitled to qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: This is the First Circuit decision that actually establishes the objectively reasonable suspicion threshold for taking a child into emergency protective custody, the standard later applied in Tower v. Leslie-Brown.
key_cases.quote: Because the welfare of the child is paramount, an objectively reasonable suspicion of abuse justifies protective measures.

state_agency.name: Division for Children, Youth and Families
state_agency.hotline: 1-800-894-5533 (in-state only) or 603-271-6562; DCYF Central Intake is staffed 24 hours a day, including weekends and holidays

mandatory_reporters: Any person (universal mandatory reporting) — N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 169-C:29
Physicians, surgeons, county medical examiners, psychiatrists, residents, interns
Registered nurses and hospital personnel (admission, examination, care and treatment)
Teachers, school officials, school nurses, school counselors
Social workers, day care workers, and any other child or foster care workers
reporting_details: New Hampshire is a universal-reporter state: RSA 169-C:29 lists physicians, dentists, psychologists, registered nurses and hospital personnel, teachers, school officials and school nurses, social workers, day care and other child or foster care workers, law enforcement officials and clergy, and closes with “any other person having reason to suspect that a child has been abused or neglected,” all of whom “shall report the same in accordance with this chapter.” RSA 169-C:30 sets the route and the form: an oral report “shall be made immediately by telephone or otherwise, and followed within 48 hours by a report in writing, if so requested, to the department” — the Department of Health and Human Services, which takes reports through the DCYF Central Intake Unit at 603-271-6562 or 1-800-894-5533 (in-state only), staffed 24 hours a day including weekends and holidays.
